title: Evidence-Based Update on the Surgical Technique and Clinical Outcomes of Retrograde Drilling: A Systematic Review
question: How strong and how consistent is the published evidence on retrograde drilling for osteochondral lesions of the talus?

bottom_line.question: How strong and how consistent is the published evidence on retrograde drilling for osteochondral lesions of the talus?
bottom_line.answer: Across 10 small, mostly low-quality studies, the mean AOFAS ankle score rose from 57.9 to 86.1 points after retrograde drilling, but weak study designs and inconsistent reporting prevent firm conclusions about its effectiveness.

provenance.quote: The 10 studies which used the AOFAS score described that the weighted mean AOFAS score improved from 57.9 points preoperatively to 86.1 points

sections.title: The Problem and Why It Needed Another Look
sections.markdown:
## The problem: damaged cartilage in the ankle

The talus is the bone at the bottom of the ankle joint, and the shin bone rests on it. Cartilage covers its surface, and beneath that cartilage is a layer called the subchondral bone. An **osteochondral lesion of the talus (OLT)** is damage to both layers, usually after an injury. It is one of the most common cartilage problems in the ankle. An earlier review found that about half of symptomatic lesions did not resolve with non-surgical care, while surgery produced good-to-excellent results in roughly 85% of patients.

Surgeons can choose from several operations, and none has been shown to outperform the others. This review covers one of them. In **retrograde drilling**, the surgeon comes at the lesion from behind, drilling up through the bone toward the damaged area without passing through the joint surface. The aim is to restore blood supply to the subchondral bone and trigger new bone growth while leaving the overlying cartilage alone. This suits cases where the cartilage is still intact and only the bone beneath it is damaged. The procedure was first described for the knee in 1981 and applied to the ankle in 1999.

## Why look again

A previous systematic review of 80 cases reported success rates of 68% to 90% for retrograde drilling. However, the studies it collected differed so much in method and reporting that their data could not be combined into one pooled estimate. The present authors set out to measure that inconsistency directly. Their hypothesis was that the published studies on retrograde drilling for OLT are heterogeneous, meaning they differ too much from one another to be compared fairly.

sections.title: How the Review Was Done
sections.markdown:
A systematic review uses a search and a set of rules fixed in advance to collect every study on a question, so the authors do not simply pick the papers they like. Two orthopedic foot and ankle surgeons followed PRISMA, the standard reporting checklist for such reviews. They searched four databases (MEDLINE, Web of Science, EMBASE and the Cochrane Library) for papers published from January 1996 to August 27, 2022, and checked the reference lists of relevant studies by hand.

A study qualified if it reported clinical outcomes of retrograde drilling for OLT, appeared in a peer-reviewed journal, and was written in English. The reviewers excluded animal and lab studies, case reports, reviews, studies with fewer than five patients, and studies that did not report results for the ankle separately. When the two reviewers disagreed, a senior author decided.

Each study was graded two ways. **Level of evidence** (LoE) ranks study design: level 1 is the strongest and level 4 is a case series with no comparison group. Quality of evidence (QoE) was measured with the Modified Coleman Methodology Score, a checklist scored out of 100 that rates how well a study was designed and reported. The authors used a version adapted for this type of ankle surgery. Scores fall into four bands:

- Excellent: 85 to 100
- Good: 70 to 84
- Fair: 55 to 69
- Poor: below 55

From each study the reviewers then recorded a fixed list of details: how the lesion was diagnosed and classified, its size and location, any cysts, how the drill was guided, the drill's width, whether bone graft was added, the rehabilitation plan, outcomes and complications.

sections.title: What They Found: Weak Evidence, Varied Practice and Outcomes
sections.markdown:
## What they found

The search turned up 189 studies. Only 11 met the criteria, and together they covered 207 ankles. Patients averaged 34.4 years old and 53% were male. Average follow-up was 31.1 months, ranging from 8 to 69 months, and no study followed patients for longer than five years.

The evidence was weak. Nine of the 11 studies were level 4 and two were level 3, giving a mean level of 3.8. The mean quality score was 50.8 (range 43 to 62). Eight studies (72.7%) rated poor and three (27.3%) rated fair. None reached good or excellent.

Inconsistency showed up at nearly every stage of care. Before surgery, the time patients spent on non-surgical treatment varied from study to study, and only six studies said what that treatment was.

Diagnosis relied on at least two imaging methods in every study: plain X-rays in all 11, MRI in 10, CT in one, and arthroscopy (a camera inserted into the joint) in 10. Nine studies classified their lesions, but they used different systems, and five used two or three systems at once. Seven used an arthroscopic classification and six used an MRI-based one, and even these did not match between studies.

The lesions were mostly on the inner side of the talus. Of the 138 lesions with a reported location, 118 were medial (inner side), 10 central and 10 lateral. Only five studies reported lesion size, some as area on MRI and some as diameter on CT. With one exception, all lesions were under 15 mm across or under 150 square mm in area. Three studies mentioned cysts in the bone under the lesion, and none reported the cysts' size.

In the operation itself, 10 studies examined the joint with arthroscopy before drilling. All guided the drill with fluoroscopy (live X-ray imaging), and one added 3D computer-assisted navigation. Drill width varied widely: five studies used drills of 2 mm or less, three used 3 to 5 mm, and three used drills wider than 6 mm. Of the six studies using drills wider than 3 mm, four packed the holes with the patient's own bone or with artificial bone. One study added shock wave therapy after surgery.

Eight studies described rehabilitation. Most had patients moving the ankle within the first week. Partial weight-bearing began anywhere from 3 to 6 weeks after surgery, and five studies allowed full weight-bearing at 6 weeks. Four studies had patients jogging at 3 months, and four reported a return to full activity at 6 months.

## Outcomes

Ten studies used the AOFAS score (from the American Orthopedic Foot and Ankle Society), a common measure of ankle function on which higher is better. The authors averaged across studies, giving each study weight in proportion to its number of patients. On that basis, scores rose from 57.9 before surgery to 86.1 at follow-up:

average improvement = 86.1 - 57.9 = 28.2 points

This is a sizable gain, measured about two and a half years after surgery on average.

Eight studies checked healing with MRI after surgery. Most described the lesions as "improved" or "healed" in general terms, without measuring changes in the bone underneath. Only one study reported return to sport (at 6 months for all its patients). Complications were rare. Among 191 ankles in the nine studies that reported complications, three patients had reduced sensation in the foot and one had a superficial wound infection.

sections.title: What the Inconsistencies Mean
sections.markdown:
The authors' central point is that these results cannot be fairly compared or pooled, because the studies differ in whom they treated, how they operated and how they measured success. This puts them at odds with another systematic review from 2023, which judged retrograde drilling effective based on the same literature. The present authors read that literature as too inconsistent and too low in quality to support such a judgment.

For each gap, they compare practice with the 2018 statements of the International Consensus Meeting on Cartilage Repair of the Ankle (ICCRA), an expert panel. For non-surgical care, ICCRA recommends 4 to 6 weeks of immobilization with only light weight-bearing for an acute, undisplaced lesion, and expects improvement over 3 to 6 months. None of the included studies described its protocol in enough detail to check against this.

Diagnosis was the one area of agreement. Studies consistently combined X-rays with MRI or CT, and used arthroscopy to confirm the main reason to choose retrograde drilling: a lesion in the bone with intact cartilage over it.

Medial lesions made up 86% of cases here, compared with roughly 70% to 77% in other reviews. The authors suggest that some surgeons drilled only medial lesions, and that lateral lesions are more often superficial injuries.

Only 45% of studies reported lesion size, although size is the main factor in deciding whether bone marrow stimulation methods (the family that retrograde drilling belongs to) are suitable. One review recommends these methods for lesions under 10.2 mm in diameter and 107.4 square mm in area. ICCRA advises bone grafting for lesions more than 1 cm wide or deep, or with cysts larger than 100 cubic mm. Because no study reported cyst size, it is unclear how the grafting decisions were made.

Aiming the drill is hard, and some reports say it misses the lesion in up to 20% of cases. Guidance options exist (3D navigation, MRI guidance, electromagnetic navigation), but most studies relied on fluoroscopy plus arthroscopy, and ICCRA considers computer or robot navigation unnecessary. The authors point out that fluoroscopy does not always show the lesion clearly, and that aiming devices can be too bulky for the ankle and injure cartilage. They call for a simple, widely available way to aim accurately.

Drill width matters because repaired cartilage tends to wear down over time after bone marrow stimulation, and damage to the underlying bone may be one cause. In a cadaver study, 1 to 1.25 mm holes harmed the bone less than 2 mm holes, and ICCRA recommends a 1 to 2 mm wire. From their own experience, the authors warn that thin drills can bend or break in the hard bone of young patients, so the best width is still an open question.

On grafting, some studies filled the drill holes with bone graft or bone substitutes and reported good results. Others drilled alone and also reported good results. Bone void substitutes flow into irregular, saucer-shaped cysts that solid graft is hard to fit into, but no study has compared the two directly.

Rehabilitation timing also varied. ICCRA suggests protecting the lesion from shearing forces for 3 months, starting sport-specific training at 3 to 6 months, and returning to competition at 6 to 12 months.

sections.title: Limitations and the Takeaway
sections.markdown:
## Limitations

The search ended almost a year before publication. The authors note this is normal, since one analysis found an average gap of 13.2 months between search and publication for systematic reviews. Most included studies were retrospective case series with few patients and short-to-medium follow-up, which raises the risk of bias. The AOFAS score, the most common outcome measure, has never been validated specifically for retrograde drilling in OLT, so it may overstate or understate the benefit. Newer approaches, such as adding stem cells taken from fat tissue or using needle-thin arthroscopes, were outside the review's scope.

## The takeaway

On the surface, retrograde drilling looks good: function scores rise by about 28 points and complications are rare. However, the evidence comes from 11 small, mostly poor-quality studies that described patients, lesions, surgery and recovery in ways that cannot be lined up against each other, and none followed patients beyond five years. The authors conclude that the technique's effectiveness cannot yet be confirmed. They call for well-designed clinical trials with standard criteria for choosing patients, classifying lesions, performing the surgery and managing rehabilitation, and with validated outcome measures, so that clinical practice guidelines for retrograde drilling can be written.

sources.abstract:
Background: Retrograde drilling is an established surgical technique to treat osteochondral lesions of the talus (OLT). It involves non-trans-articular drilling to induce subchondral bone revascularization and bone formation without damaging the overlying articular cartilage. The present study aimed to elucidate the heterogeneity of clinical studies on retrograde drilling for OLT.

Design: A systematic search of the MEDLINE, Web of Science, EMBASE, and Cochrane Library databases for studies published between January 1996 and August 27, 2022, was performed based on the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines by two independent reviewers. The included studies were evaluated for their level of evidence (LoE) and quality of evidence (QoE) using the Modified Coleman Methodology Score. Variables reporting surgical and clinical outcomes and complications were evaluated.

Results: Eleven studies with 207 ankles were included (mean follow-up period = 31.1 months). The mean LoE was 3.8 (LoE 3: two studies, LoE 4: nine studies), and the mean QoE was 50.8 (fair: three studies, poor: eight studies). Ten studies used the American Orthopedic Foot and Ankle Society (AOFAS) score, which improved from 57.9 preoperatively to 86.1 postoperatively. The period and protocol of conservative treatment, lesion character, surgical technique, and postoperative protocol were inconsistent or underreported.

Conclusions: This systematic review revealed that low LoE and poor QoE, coupled with heterogeneity among the included studies, impede definitive conclusions regarding the effectiveness of this technique. Consequently, well-designed clinical trials are essential to develop standardized clinical guidelines for using retrograde drilling in OLT.
sources.section19-19476035241239303/p1: The present systematic review established the heterogeneity in clinical studies on retrograde drilling for OLT. Since there was underreporting of data regarding classification systems, surgical technique, and postoperative protocols, a comparison of results was not possible. Therefore, there is a need for standardized guidelines for diagnosis, treatment techniques, and postoperative rehabilitation for OLT. A majority (82%) of the included studies were classified as LoE = 4, and none of the studies could be classified as excellent or good quality. These findings highlight the need to re-evaluate the evidence upon which standard paradigms and prognostic indicators for OLT are based. In addition, our review acknowledges and contrasts with the findings of another recent systematic review published in 2023, which concluded the efficacy of retrograde drilling for OLT based on existing literature. Our analysis distinctively highlights the lack of reproducibility and methodological rigor in these studies due to their heterogeneity, leading us to a different conclusion from the aforementioned review. By identifying these gaps, our review complements and broadens the scope of the current literature, offering a more comprehensive and nuanced understanding of the effectiveness of retrograde drilling.
sources.section19-19476035241239303/p5: There were some interesting revelations regarding the lesion character. First, there was general agreement among studies regarding the location of the lesions, with medial lesions accounting for the majority (86%). A recent systematic review revealed that medial lesions accounted for approximately 70% of OLTs, while another systematic review by Dahmen et al. reported a 77% incidence for medial lesions. A probable reason for the significantly higher incidence of medial OLTs in the present systematic review may be due to the surgeon’s policy of performing retrograde drilling only on medial lesions in the included studies,, and the fact that lateral lesions are more prone to superficial injury than medial lesions. Second, the classification of OLTs varied among the included studies. Although all included studies evaluated articular cartilage properties and performed retrograde drilling, the variability in disease classification systems makes it challenging to compare results across studies. To date, many classifications for OLT have been proposed. Therefore, the ICCRA tried to establish a comprehensive classification in 2019; however, the consensus statement announced that it was difficult to establish a comprehensive classification system for OLT over the course of a single meeting. Third, we observed that 45% of the included studies described the lesion size. Traditionally, retrograde drilling is classified as a bone marrow stimulation technique in which the size of the OLT is the most critical in determining whether bone marrow stimulation is indicated. A systematic review by Ramponi et al. in 2016 reported that bone marrow stimulation is recommended for lesions measuring <10.2 mm in diameter and 107.4 mm2 in the area. Further research is warranted to clarify whether lesion size would affect the surgical outcomes in the OLTs treated with retrograde drilling. sources.section5-19476035241239303/p1: Osteochondral lesion of the talus (OLT) is a common cartilage disorder of the ankle, typically resulting from traumatic damage to the articular cartilage and subchondral bone. A systematic review published in 2010 identified that 50% of the primary symptomatic OLTs failed to resolve using conservative treatment, and operative management, including reparative procedures, was most effective with good-to-excellent clinical outcomes in about 85% of the patients. Various surgical techniques, such as bone marrow stimulation, retrograde drilling, osteochondral transplantation, cartilage implantation, and chondrogenesis techniques, are available for treating OLTs; however, it has been reported that none of these techniques was superior to others. Despite the satisfactory outcomes of operative treatment, there are long-term clinical concerns regarding the biological deterioration of the repair.
sources.section5-19476035241239303/p2: Retrograde drilling is a well-known non-trans-articular procedure to induce subchondral bone revascularization and bone formation without disrupting the already damaged talar articular cartilage in OLT. Lee and Mercurioin first described this reparative procedure for knee lesions in 1981, and later, Taranow applied it to the ankle joint in 1999. Eventually, Dahman et al. reported a 68% to 90% success rate of the procedure in a systematic review based on 80 cases of OLT. However, despite the substantial success rates, the authors mentioned that the heterogeneity in the included studies did not allow for pooling. Consequently, homogeneous reporting of outcome data is essential, which allows the pooling and comparison of results to propose and establish clinically relevant guidelines.
